title: Grade 10 learners' foundational knowledge gaps in accounting: Views of accounting teachers in Pinetown district in Kwazulu-Natal
text_snippet: Grade 10 learners' foundational knowledge gaps in accounting: Views of accounting teachers in Pinetown district in Kwazulu-Natal As in many other disciplines, accounting education is made up of ever-more complex building blocks, such that prior years’ knowledge serves as the foundation for future learning. Meanwhile, the literature indicates that the lack of foundational knowledge among Grade 10 accounting learners in South African secondary schools affect their academic experiences. As part of a larger project to develop and implement interventions to build the capacity of accounting teachers, this paper explored the views of Grade 10 accounting teachers in the Pinetown District of South Africa, to explain the knowledge gap among learners. Based on attribution theory, a qualitative case study design was employed to conduct a thematic analysis of the views of eight teachers in a focus group interview. The findings attributed the knowledge gap mainly to Grade 10 curriculum overload, deficiencies in foundational accounting knowledge from prior years, and other factors within teachers’ control. title: Exploring first-year pre-service teachers ’conceptual understanding of isometric drawing in engineering graphics and design
text_snippet: Exploring first-year pre-service teachers ’conceptual understanding of isometric drawing in engineering graphics and design The persistent challenges in teaching and learning isometric drawing stem from the complex demands of spatial visualisation and the difficulty in transforming two-dimensional (2D) representations into three-dimensional (3D) mental models. These challenges have raised concerns across educational and professional spheres, prompting the need for in-depth research and innovative solutions. This mixed-methods study explored the spatial visualisation abilities and misconceptions that first-year engineering graphics and design (EGD) pre-service teachers demonstrate when applying isometric projection principles. Forty first-year EGD pre-service teachers were purposively sampled and subjected to a comprehensive freehand isometric drawing assessment comprising ten tasks of varying complexity to assess their conceptual understanding and application of isometric projection principles. The quantitative data (task scores) were analysed using the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) to determine the mean and standard deviation. title: The impact of hybrid teaching methods on student engagement in cosmetology courses
text_snippet: The impact of hybrid teaching methods on student engagement in cosmetology courses The cosmetic industry in Indonesia, identified as a national priority sector, continues to grow rapidly due to increased health awareness and rising income levels. Furthermore, universities are expected to produce graduates with industry-specific competencies. This study examined the implementation of student- and teacher-centred learning methods in a cosmetology course in the Department of Pharmacy at Atma Jaya Catholic University of Indonesia. This study employed a within-subjects research design to compare the impact of teacher- and student-centred instructional methods in the same cohort of 44 pharmacy students. Data were collected at the end of the 14-week course using a structured questionnaire consisting of nine closed-ended questions and one open-ended question. Student-centred methods, including case studies and group discussions, were perceived to enhance student engagement and knowledge acquisition. The survey results showed that 70.45% of the respondents found assignments clear, 63.63% reported increased knowledge, and 59.09% appreciated group discussions. title: Professional discretion and the prevention of negligence: Perspectives from educators in South African public schools
text_snippet: Professional discretion and the prevention of negligence: Perspectives from educators in South African public schools This article expands upon research in the realm of educators’ professional discretion concerning the prevention of negligence in South African public schools. The literature indicates that many educators remain unaware of how the law relates to policy obligations and in loco parentis responsibilities, as evidenced by the increasing number of legal cases and the expanding scope of educators’ negligence responsibilities. This study investigated methods through which educators can harmonise their professional discretion with their legal and policy obligations to mitigate negligence. Applying Dworkin’s (1978) ‘doughnut’ metaphor to professional discretion as a conceptual framework, the study employed a qualitative research approach within an interpretive paradigm. Twenty participants in semi-structured interviews and a review of pertinent court cases were used in the data collection process. The findings suggested that participants generally shared similar views on the root causes of negligence in educational settings. title: Quality assurance in South African independent schools: Perceptions, challenges and the role of Umalusi in enhancing teaching and learning
text_snippet: Quality assurance in South African independent schools: Perceptions, challenges and the role of Umalusi in enhancing teaching and learning Research on educational quality assurance (QA) in South Africa has largely overlooked the independent schooling sector, focusing instead on public schools. Addressing this gap, this article reports on a study which examined the impact of Umalusi’s QA and accreditation process on four principals, four heads of department and eight teachers from four independent schools in South Africa. The research reveals a system that primarily functions as a mechanism of enforced standardisation. Through semi-structured interviews with participants, key findings indicate that the process triggers intentional, ritualistic compliance and window-dressing without integrating QA into their core teaching practices. While the accreditation certificate is valued as a symbol of legitimacy, the process itself is perceived as an administrative burden that exacerbates inequity for lower-fee schools and has no discernible impact on teaching and learning. The study concludes that Umalusi’s current model, by prioritising standardisation over genuine improvement, fosters a counterproductive culture of ceremonial compliance and fails to enhance educational quality.

title: Legal and educational implications of teacher post reductions in South Africa: A focus on the Western Cape
text_snippet: Legal and educational implications of teacher post reductions in South Africa: A focus on the Western Cape The decision to reduce teacher posts in South Africa, and in the Western Cape in particular, has provoked concern regarding legal compliance, the effect on the quality of education, and the question of equity. This study explored the legal and educational implications of teacher post-decrement using a qualitative desktop research approach. It analysed national legislation, policy documents, court decisions, government reports, academic literature, and selected media reports related to post-provisioning and labour relations in the public schooling sector. The study aimed to examine provincial education departments’ compliance with legal obligations and the role teacher unions play in advocating for teachers’ rights. The analysis indicated that budgetary constraints and declining learner enrolment are often used to justify post-cutbacks. These explanations raise serious questions about adherence to constitutional, national educational and labour law requirements, including the South African Schools Act, the Employment of Educators Act, and section 29(1)(a) of the Constitution. title: Experiences of South African primary school teachers fostering practical education for sustainable development activities: a PAR approach
text_snippet: Experiences of South African primary school teachers fostering practical education for sustainable development activities: a PAR approach This paper presents the experiences of primary school teachers engaged in a participatory action research project aimed at fostering education for sustainable development (ESD), with a focus on practical examples of ESD in and around the school premises. The primary objectives of this paper are to share the teachers’ experiences and elucidate how they incorporate ESD into their teaching and learning activities. The primary data-gathering method employed in this study involves reflective essays complemented by recorded discussions throughout various stages of the action research project. Thematic analysis of the discussions unveiled a strong inclination among primary school teachers to integrate ESD in their classrooms and instigate positive change in their communities. This paper incorporates illustrative examples of practical classroom ESD activities. These examples encompass the use of waste digesters and colour-coded bins for segregating various types of waste. The findings emphasise the enthusiasm demonstrated by both teachers and learners towards ESD, revealing a shared desire to contribute to positive change in their school community.

title: Using questioning strategies to support pre-service teachers in teaching mathematics word problem-solving
text_snippet: Using questioning strategies to support pre-service teachers in teaching mathematics word problem-solving This empirical paper reports on the use of questioning strategies that enabled pre-service foundation phase teachers (PSFPTs) to enhance their mathematics word-problem-solving instruction. The objective of the study was to determine how PSFPTs used questioning strategies as proverbial keys to unlock meaning from word problems and to support their teaching of mathematics word problem solving. Using a qualitative research approach within the constructivist paradigm, the study employed a multiple-case study design embedded in the lesson study process (LSD). At the same time, Desimone’s core conceptual framework for professional development served as the conceptual framework. Twelve second year PSFPTs were purposefully selected from a university in the Gauteng Province. As part of LSD, data were generated through collaboratively developed lesson plans, video-recorded lessons, observation checklists and collaborative discussions. The data were analysed inductively through thematic analysis. title: Reflective practice in action: Enhancing physics tutoring in post-apartheid South africa's evolving educational landscape
text_snippet: Reflective practice in action: Enhancing physics tutoring in post-apartheid South africa's evolving educational landscape This article reports on a study exploring the role of reflective practice among physics tutors at a tertiary institution in post-apartheid South Africa. Grounded in constructivism, reflective practice, and situational activity theory, the study examines how tutors’ reflective engagement shapes their pedagogical approaches and supports learning among historically disadvantaged students. A phenomenographic research design was employed, drawing on tutorial observations to capture real-time practices, semi-structured interviews to explore tutors’ reflections on their roles, and video recordings used both as data sources and reflective tools. The findings reveal varied conceptualisations of tutoring roles, with tutors positioning themselves as learning facilitators and knowledge mediators. Tutors who engaged more consistently in reflective practice demonstrated greater adaptability and effectiveness in fostering conceptual understanding. However, sustained reflective engagement was constrained by time pressures, limited formal training, emotional resistance, and institutional isolation.
